name: Simon the governor of the temple
charge: Betraying the temple treasury to the king out of a private quarrel; slandering Onias the high priest
summary: Simon of the tribe of Benjamin was made governor of the temple, and when he could not prevail against Onias in a quarrel over the disorder of the city he went to the nations and reported the treasury as money lying there for the king. After Heliodorus was driven off, he slandered Onias as the worker of those evils and called a traitor the man who had deserved well of the city, and murders were committed by men of his faction. Onias went to the king seeking the good of all rather than to accuse his countrymen, and the record gives no sentence upon Simon.
offenseFull: Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about the disorder of the city (2 Maccabees 3:4). The class read out what that office carried: management of the temple resources, maintenance of the temple, administration of the worship, the handling of disputes, coordination with the other authorities, and security. Whatever the dispute was, Onias as high priest had the last say. When Simon could not overcome him he got him to Apollonius, the governor of Coelosyria and Phenice, and told him the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money (2 Maccabees 3:5-6). He ran to the other nations. They were working together on that temple, and because of one argument he carried the nations against the man set over him. One man had a problem with one man, and because he could not have his way he thought to tear down the whole nation.

The class measures the offense by the proverbs read with it. Every friend says he is a friend, but there is a friend which is only a friend in name, and it is a grief to death when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy (Ecclesiasticus 37:1-4). Offend not against the multitude of a city; bind not one sin upon another, for in one you shall not go unpunished; and say not that God will look upon the multitude of your offerings, as though a man may sin on purpose and be forgiven anyway (Ecclesiasticus 7:7-9). The money he exposed was for the widows, the orphans, the strangers and the Levites, and the bread of the needy is their life, so that he who takes away his neighbour’s living slays him (Ecclesiasticus 34:21-22). Three things the wise man said his heart feared are the slander of a city, the gathering together of an unruly multitude, and a false accusation, all of them worse than death (Ecclesiasticus 26:5-7). Simon did all three: he slandered the city, he gathered the Greeks to get the money out of Jerusalem, and he falsely accused Onias.
judgmentFull: When the seizure failed, Simon, having been a betrayer of the money and of his country, slandered Onias as if he had terrified Heliodorus and been the worker of these evils, and was so bold as to call a traitor the man who had deserved well of the city, tendered his own nation and was zealous of the laws; and their hatred went so far that murders were committed by one of his faction (2 Maccabees 4:1-3). The class reading this in another year puts the killing plainly: men under Simon took it upon themselves to go and kill men who were with Onias, and they had that spirit because it was the spirit on the man over them. That is the pattern traced through the whole lesson: he coveted the upper hand, from there it turned to anger, from there to slander, and from there to murder, one sin knocking over the next. Wars and fightings come out of lusts that war in a man, who kills and desires to have and cannot obtain, and asks amiss (James 4:1-3); a man angry with his brother without a cause is in danger of the judgment, and the name calling carries the sin further (Matthew 5:21-22); and a man who hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15). The men who saw it and said nothing were not clear either, since a witness who hears and does not utter it bears the iniquity (Leviticus 5:1), and he that is partner with a thief hates his own soul (Proverbs 29:24).

Onias, seeing the danger of this contention, and that Apollonius as governor did rage and increase Simon’s malice, went to the king, not as an accuser of his countrymen but seeking the good of all, both publicly and privately, because he saw it was impossible for the state to continue quiet or for Simon to leave his folly unless the king looked to it (2 Maccabees 4:4-6). Blessed are the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), and a man is to live peaceably with all men as much as lies in him (Romans 12:18), but the qualifier is there for a reason; some spirits do not want peace, and some men cannot be reasoned with, because all men have not faith (2 Thessalonians 3:1-2). No sentence upon Simon is written. Three years afterward his brother Menelaus bought the priesthood, so that the high priest of Israel was now of the tribe of Benjamin (2 Maccabees 4:23-24), and what Simon set in motion went on working after him.

text.text: But one Simon of the tribe of Benjamin, who was made governor of the temple, fell out with the high priest about disorder in the city.
And when he could not overcome Onias, he gat him to Apollonius the son of Thraseas, who then was governor of Celosyria and Phenice,

And told him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of infinite sums of money, so that the multitude of their riches, which did not pertain to the account of the sacrifices, was innumerable, and that it was possible to bring all into the king’s hand.
Every friend saith, I am his friend also: but there is a friend, which is only a friend in name.
Is it not a grief unto death, when a companion and friend is turned to an enemy?
O wicked imagination, whence camest thou in to cover the earth with deceit?
There is a companion, which rejoiceth in the prosperity of a friend, but in the time of trouble will be against him.
Offend not against the multitude of a city, and then thou shalt not cast thyself down among the people.
Bind not one sin upon another; for in one thou shalt not be unpunished.
Say not, God will look upon the multitude of my oblations, and when I offer to the most high God, he will accept it.
The bread of the needy is their life: he that defraudeth him thereof is a man of blood.
He that taketh away his neighbour’s living slayeth him; and he that defraudeth the labourer of his hire is a bloodshedder.

There be three things that mine heart feareth; and for the fourth I was sore afraid: the slander of a city, the gathering together of an unruly multitude, and a false accusation: all these are worse than death.
But a grief of heart and sorrow is a woman that is jealous over another woman, and a scourge of the tongue which communicateth with all.
An evil wife is a yoke shaken to and fro: he that hath hold of her is as though he held a scorpion.
This Simon now, of whom we spake afore, having been a betrayer of the money, and of his country, slandered Onias, as if he had terrified Heliodorus, and been the worker of these evils.
Thus was he bold to call him a traitor, that had deserved well of the city, and tendered his own nation, and was so zealous of the laws.
But when their hatred went so far, that by one of Simon’s faction murders were committed,
From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?
Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.
Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.
Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment:

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.
And if a soul sin, and hear the voice of swearing, and is a witness, whether he hath seen or known of it; if he do not utter it, then he shall bear his iniquity.
Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not.
Onias seeing the danger of this contention, and that Apollonius, as being the governor of Celosyria and Phenice, did rage, and increase Simon’s malice,
He went to the king, not to be an accuser of his countrymen, but seeking the good of all, both publick and private:
For he saw that it was impossible that the state should continue quiet, and Simon leave his folly, unless the king did look thereunto.
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified, even as it is with you:
And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith.
Three years afterward Jason sent Menelaus, the aforesaid Simon’s brother, to bear the money unto the king, and to put him in mind of certain necessary matters.

But he being brought to the presence of the king, when he had magnified him for the glorious appearance of his power, got the priesthood to himself, offering more than Jason by three hundred talents of silver.
Thou shalt not raise a false report: put not thine hand with the wicked to be an unrighteous witness.
Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. And all the people shall say, Amen.
